claim: Cranial irradiation is used for prophylactic brain radiotherapy as well as the treatment of primary brain tumors.
source: Cranial irradiation is used for prophylactic brain radiotherapy as well as the treatment of primary brain tumors.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical practice presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Cranial irradiation often induces unexpected side effects, including cognitive dysfunction.
source: Despite its high efficiency, it often induces unexpected side effects, including cognitive dysfunction.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mice exposed to cranial irradiation exhibited cognitive dysfunction, including altered spontaneous behavior, decreased spatial memory, and reduced novel object recognition.
source: Herein, we observed that mice exposed to cranial irradiation exhibited cognitive dysfunction, including altered spontaneous behavior, decreased spatial memory, and reduced novel object recognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data presented in Figure 1B and 1C showing reduced spontaneous alteration, time in novel arm, and novel object recognition.

claim: Ionizing radiation disrupted the filamentous/globular actin (F/G-actin) ratio.
source: Analysis of the actin cytoskeleton revealed that ionizing radiation (IR) disrupted the filamentous/globular actin (F/G-actin) ratio and downregulated the actin turnover signaling pathway p21-activated kinase 3 (PAK3)-LIM kinase 1 (LIMK1)-cofilin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating decreased F/G-actin ratios in cortical neurons, frontal cortex, and hippocampus after IR.

claim: Ionizing radiation downregulated the PAK3-LIMK1-cofilin signaling pathway.
source: Analysis of the actin cytoskeleton revealed that ionizing radiation (IR) disrupted the filamentous/globular actin (F/G-actin) ratio and downregulated the actin turnover signaling pathway p21-activated kinase 3 (PAK3)-LIM kinase 1 (LIMK1)-cofilin.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2E and 2H showing decreased phosphorylated LIMK1 and cofilin after IR.

claim: IR could upregulate microRNA-206-3p (miR-206-3p) targeting PAK3.
source: Furthermore, we found that IR could upregulate microRNA-206–3 p (miR-206–3 p) targeting PAK3.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5C and 5D showing increased miR-206-3p expression after IR in both mouse and human neurons.

claim: Inhibition of miR-206-3p through antagonist (antagomiR) restored IR-induced disruption of PAK3 signaling.
source: As the inhibition of miR-206–3 p through antagonist (antagomiR), IR-induced disruption of PAK3 signaling is restored.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5E and 5G showing restoration of PAK3 levels and downstream signaling after antagomiR treatment.

claim: Intranasal administration of antagomiR-206-3p recovered IR-induced cognitive impairment in mice.
source: In addition, intranasal administration of antagomiR-206–3 p recovered IR-induced cognitive impairment in mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data in Figure 6E and 6F showing improved cognitive performance after antagomiR treatment.

claim: The cumulative risk of brain metastasis within 1 year was 14.6% in the PCI group and 40.4% in the non-PCI group for small-cell lung cancer patients.
source: Notably, in the case of small-cell lung cancer, the cumulative risk of brain metastasis within 1 year was 14.6% in the PCI group and 40.4% in the non-PCI group. Accordingly, the 1 year survival rate was 27.1% in the PCI group and 13.3% in the non-PCI group (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00016211, Slotman et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a clinical trial (Slotman et al., 2007).

claim: The 1 year survival rate was 27.1% in the PCI group and 13.3% in the non-PCI group for small-cell lung cancer patients.
source: Accordingly, the 1 year survival rate was 27.1% in the PCI group and 13.3% in the non-PCI group (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00016211, Slotman et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a clinical trial (Slotman et al., 2007).

claim: The side effects of PCI inevitably affect 50-90% of long-term survivors with permanent and substantial cognitive impairment.
source: However, it has been reported that the side effects of PCI inevitably affect 50–90% of long-term survivors with permanent and substantial cognitive impairment (Greene-Schloesser et al., 2013; Makale et al., 2017; Rosi et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Survivors treated with whole-brain irradiation exhibit severe impairment in memory (54.9%), processing speed (66.3%), and executive function (68.3%).
source: The survivors treated with whole-brain irradiation exhibit severe impairment in memory (54.9%), processing speed (66.3%), and executive function (68.3%) (Brinkman et al., 2016; Krull et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Brinkman et al., 2016; Krull et al., 2013).

claim: In IR-treated mice, spontaneous alteration was significantly reduced by 66.67%.
source: In mice treated with IR, spontaneous alteration and time in the novel arm were significantly reduced by 66.67% and 58.14%, respectively (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Y-maze behavioral tests shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In IR-treated mice, time in the novel arm was significantly reduced by 58.14%.
source: In mice treated with IR, spontaneous alteration and time in the novel arm were significantly reduced by 66.67% and 58.14%, respectively (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Y-maze spatial memory tests shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The time spent with objects did not differ between familiar and novel objects in IR-treated mice.
source: The time spent with objects did not differ between familiar and novel objects in IR-treated mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IR-treated mice exhibited reduced time in the center of the OPF, thereby indicating depressive-like behavior.
source: IR-treated mice exhibited reduced time in the center of the OPF, thereby indicating depressive-like behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In IR-treated neurons, mature dendritic spines (mushroom) were significantly decreased by 37.5%.
source: In IR-treated neurons, mature dendritic spines (mushroom) were significantly decreased by 37.5%, whereas immature dendritic spines (filopodia) were increased by 37.14% (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In IR-treated neurons, immature dendritic spines (filopodia) were increased by 37.14%.
source: In IR-treated neurons, mature dendritic spines (mushroom) were significantly decreased by 37.5%, whereas immature dendritic spines (filopodia) were increased by 37.14% (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Exposure to IR decreased the F/G-actin ratio in cortical neurons by 21.05%.
source: Exposure to IR decreased the F/G-actin ratio in cortical neurons (21.05%), frontal cortex (21.74%), and hippocampus (73.91%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Exposure to IR decreased the F/G-actin ratio in frontal cortex by 21.74%.
source: Exposure to IR decreased the F/G-actin ratio in cortical neurons (21.05%), frontal cortex (21.74%), and hippocampus (73.91%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Exposure to IR decreased the F/G-actin ratio in hippocampus by 73.91%.
source: Exposure to IR decreased the F/G-actin ratio in cortical neurons (21.05%), frontal cortex (21.74%), and hippocampus (73.91%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PAK3 gene showed a 0.5-fold altered expression in the irradiated brain.
source: Among the 15 coding genes that were up- and downregulated by cranial irradiation, we focused on the PAK3 gene, which showed a 0.5-fold altered expression in the irradiated brain, considering both the 'synapse organization' and the 'dendritic spine development' ontologies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 2A from a previous study (GSE94440).

claim: IR decreased mRNA level of PAK3 in cortical neurons by 49.48%.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, IR decreased mRNA and protein levels of PAK3 in cortical neurons (49.48% and 44.30%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IR decreased protein level of PAK3 in cortical neurons by 44.30%.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, IR decreased mRNA and protein levels of PAK3 in cortical neurons (49.48% and 44.30%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IR decreased mRNA level of PAK3 in frontal cortex by 61.67%.
source: In addition, IR decreased mRNA level of PAK3 in frontal cortex (61.67%) and hippocampus (66.67%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IR decreased mRNA level of PAK3 in hippocampus by 66.67%.
source: In addition, IR decreased mRNA level of PAK3 in frontal cortex (61.67%) and hippocampus (66.67%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PAK3 was localized on dendrites in cortical neurons.
source: Based on immunocytochemistry data, PAK3 was localized on dendrites in cortical neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IR decreased the expression of phosphorylated LIMK1 and cofilin in cortical neurons, frontal cortex, and hippocampus.
source: Herein, we observed that IR decreased the expression of phosphorylated LIMK1 and cofilin in cortical neurons, frontal cortex, and hippocampus (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E and 2H.

claim: Phosphorylated LIMK1 and cofilin were less expressed and localized on the dendrites in cortical neurons after IR.
source: In addition, phosphorylated LIMK1 and cofilin were less expressed and localized on the dendrites in cortical neurons (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: IR did not alter other downstream factors related to cytoskeleton regulation, such as OP18 and tubulin-folding cofactor B (TBCB).
source: However, IR did not alter other downstream factors related to cytoskeleton regulation, such as OP18 and tubulin-folding cofactor B (TBCB) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Every two shRNAs targeting PAK3 successfully reduced the mRNA level of PAK3 by approximately 30%.
source: Every two shRNAs targeting PAK3 successfully reduced the mRNA level of PAK3 by approximately 30% (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Downregulated PAK3 expression reduced the F/G-actin ratio.
source: Downregulated PAK3 expression reduced the F/G-actin ratio (Figure 3B) and LIMK1-cofilin signaling (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Downregulated PAK3 expression reduced LIMK1-cofilin signaling.
source: Downregulated PAK3 expression reduced the F/G-actin ratio (Figure 3B) and LIMK1-cofilin signaling (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The number of mushroom spines was lower than that of filopodia following PAK3 downregulation.
source: However, the number of mushroom spines was lower than that of filopodia following PAK3 downregulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PAK3 overexpression could restore IR-induced downregulation of F/G-actin.
source: Notably, PAK3 overexpression could restore IR-induced downregulation of F/G-actin (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mushroom spines were more abundant than filopodia in IR-treated PAK3 overexpressing neurons.
source: Following alterations in the F/G-actin ratio, mushroom spines were more abundant than filopodia in IR-treated PAK3 overexpressing neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: IR decreased neuronal viability in human differentiated neurons, with approximately 80% survival.
source: IR decreased neuronal viability in human differentiated neurons, with approximately 80% survival (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IR reduced the F/G-actin ratio in human differentiated neurons.
source: Consistent with previous murine neuron data, IR reduced the F/G-actin ratio (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IR decreased the expression of PAK3, phosphorylated-LIMK1, and phosphorylated-cofilin in human neurons.
source: IR decreased the expression of PAK3, phosphorylated-LIMK1, and phosphorylated-cofilin in human neurons (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: IR downregulated the mature dendritic spine and upregulated the immature dendritic spine in human neurons.
source: A previous study has revealed that IR can reduce mature dendritic spines and enhance immature dendritic spines (Figure 1D); IR downregulated the mature dendritic spine and upregulated the immature dendritic spine in human neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Downregulated PAK3 expression increased the number of immature dendritic spines in human differentiated neurons.
source: Consistent with the IR effect on dendritic spines, downregulated PAK3 expression increased the number of immature dendritic spines (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: IR failed to induce any change in luciferase activity for the Pak3 promoter in murine neurons.
source: In murine neurons, IR failed to induce any change in luciferase activity (Figure 5A), suggesting that IR does not induce PAK3 expression by regulating transcription levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: IR significantly upregulated only miR-206-3p among three miRNA candidates in both mice and humans.
source: Among the three miRNAs, IR significantly upregulated only miR-206–3 p in both mice and humans (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IR increased miR-206-3p expression in both mouse and human neurons.
source: IR increased miR-206–3 p expression in both mouse and human neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: AntagomiR-206-3p successfully inhibited IR-induced miR-206-3p expression in mouse and human neurons.
source: In addition, antagomiR-206–3 p successfully inhibited IR-induced miR-206–3 p expression in mouse and human neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: IR-induced PAK3 downregulation was restored to approximately 90% of the control in both mouse and human neurons after antagomiR treatment.
source: Consistent with the miRNA inhibition data, IR-induced PAK3 downregulation was restored to approximately 90% of the control in both neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: miR-206-3p decreased PAK signaling.
source: As expected, miR-206–3 p decreased PAK signaling, and the respective antagonist partially restored the downregulated PAK3 signaling (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: The antagonist of miR-206-3p partially restored the downregulated PAK3 signaling.
source: As expected, miR-206–3 p decreased PAK signaling, and the respective antagonist partially restored the downregulated PAK3 signaling (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: IR disrupted the distribution of dendritic spines, and IR with antagomiR treatment restored dendritic spine maturation.
source: In addition, consistent with the effects of antagomiR, IR disrupted the distribution of dendritic spines, and IR with antagomiR treatment restored dendritic spine maturation (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by dendritic spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Treatment with Cy5-antagomiR dose-dependently increased Cy5 fluorescence in the brain after intranasal administration.
source: Treatment with Cy5-antagomiR treatment dose-dependently increased Cy5 fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AntagomiR decreased the IR-induced miR-206-3p expression in the frontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: Consistent with in vitro results (Figure 5D), antagomiR decreased the IR-induced miR-206–3 p expression in the frontal cortex and hippocampus (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: IR-treated mice administered antagomiR exhibited attenuated spontaneous alteration, as well as time in the novel arm and time spent with the novel object.
source: IR-treated mice administered antagomiR exhibited attenuated spontaneous alteration, as well as time in the novel arm and time spent with the novel object (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Time spent in the center of the OPF was restored in IR-treated mice administered antagomiR.
source: In addition, time spent in the center of the OPF was restored in IR-treated mice administered antagomiR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AntagomiR treatment increased the expression of PAK3, phosphorylated-LIMK1, and phosphorylated-cofilin in the frontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: Consistently, antagomiR treatment increased the expression of PAK3, phosphorylated-LIMK1, and phosphorylated-cofilin in the frontal cortex and hippocampus (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The F/G-actin ratio in the frontal cortex and hippocampus was restored to normal when compared with that in the IR-treated group after antagomiR treatment.
source: In addition, the F/G-actin ratio in the frontal cortex and hippocampus was restored to normal when compared with that in the IR-treated group (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by F/G-actin ratio measurements shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The frontal cortex and hippocampus are two critical regions of the brain that play a key role in cognition, including memory, attention, and decision-making.
source: The frontal cortex and hippocampus are two critical regions of the brain that play a key role in cognition, including memory, attention, and decision-making (Christensen et al., 2022; Hogeveen et al., 2022; Price and Duman, 2020; Sakimoto et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and represents established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Dendritic spine morphology plays a key role in synaptic plasticity in the frontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: Cognition is closely associated with dendritic spine morphology, which plays a key role in synaptic plasticity in the frontal cortex and hippocampus (Delevich et al., 2020; Lamprecht, 2021; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and represents established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: PAK3 is a serine/threonine kinase that plays a critical role in the regulation of dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity.
source: p21-activated kinase 3 (PAK3) is a serine/threonine kinase that plays a critical role in the regulation of dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity (Combeau et al., 2012; Thévenot et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge about PAK3 function.

claim: PAK3 is highly expressed in the brain, particularly in postmitotic neurons of the cerebral cortex and the hippocampus.
source: PAK3 is highly expressed in the brain, particularly in postmitotic neurons of the cerebral cortex and the hippocampus, where it shows a diffuse distribution throughout the soma and proximal dendrites.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about PAK3 expression patterns and is consistent with the Allen Brain Map data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PAK3-deficient mice exhibit defects in the morphology of dendritic spines, which lead to impairments in synaptic plasticity and cognitive function.
source: PAK3-deficient mice exhibit defects in the morphology of dendritic spines, which lead to impairments in synaptic plasticity and cognitive function (Meng et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study (Meng et al., 2005).

claim: PAK3 is implicated in cognitive impairment in various neurological and psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Several studies have reported that PAK3 is implicated in cognitive impairment in various neurological and psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Lauterborn et al., 2020; Morrow et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions is typically delivered to the brain in patients with PCI.
source: A total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions is typically delivered to the brain in patients with PCI (Suwinski, 2021; Wegner et al., 2019), and previous studies reported that a total dose of 10 Gy caused impaired neurogenesis and cognitive behavior in mice (Pazzaglia et al., 2020; Raber et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies describing clinical PCI protocols.

claim: A total dose of 10 Gy caused impaired neurogenesis and cognitive behavior in mice.
source: A total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions is typically delivered to the brain in patients with PCI (Suwinski, 2021; Wegner et al., 2019), and previous studies reported that a total dose of 10 Gy caused impaired neurogenesis and cognitive behavior in mice (Pazzaglia et al., 2020; Raber et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies in mouse models.

claim: F-actin is a rigid, filament-like structure that provides the structural stability required for dendritic spine maturation and synaptic function.
source: F-actin is a rigid, filament-like structure that provides the structural stability required for dendritic spine maturation and synaptic function. G-actin is a monomeric form of actin that serves as the building block for F-actin and is critical for actin dynamics and the formation of new dendritic spines.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about actin biology.

claim: G-actin is a monomeric form of actin that serves as the building block for F-actin and is critical for actin dynamics and the formation of new dendritic spines.
source: G-actin is a monomeric form of actin that serves as the building block for F-actin and is critical for actin dynamics and the formation of new dendritic spines.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about actin biology.

claim: An appropriate balance between F-actin and G-actin is essential for maintaining dendritic spine structure and function.
source: An appropriate balance between F-actin and G-actin is essential for maintaining dendritic spine structure and function (Hlushchenko et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Disruptions in the F-actin/G-actin balance have been linked to cognitive dysfunction in various neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: Disruptions in this balance have been linked to cognitive dysfunction in various neurological and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This statement is based on the preceding discussion and citations about actin dynamics and cognitive function.

claim: PAK proteins function as Rac1 and Cdc42-specific effector molecules that mediate cytoskeletal remodeling by regulating LIM kinase (LIMK), oncoprotein 18 (OP18), and tubulin folding cofactor b (TBCB).
source: PAK proteins function as Rac1 and Cdc42-specific effector molecules that mediate cytoskeletal remodeling by regulating LIM kinase (LIMK), oncoprotein 18 (OP18), and tubulin folding cofactor b (TBCB) (Molli et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study (Molli et al., 2009).

claim: PAK3 phosphorylates LIMK1 to activate it.
source: PAK3 phosphorylates LIMK1 to activate it, and activated LIMK1, in turn, phosphorylates cofilin to its inactive state.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about the PAK3-LIMK1-cofilin signaling pathway, supported by citations (Edwards et al., 1999; Bamburg et al., 2021).

claim: Activated LIMK1 phosphorylates cofilin to its inactive state.
source: PAK3 phosphorylates LIMK1 to activate it, and activated LIMK1, in turn, phosphorylates cofilin to its inactive state.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about the PAK3-LIMK1-cofilin signaling pathway, supported by citations (Edwards et al., 1999; Bamburg et al., 2021).

claim: Activated cofilin promotes actin turnover, while inactivated cofilin suppresses actin turnover.
source: Activated cofilin promotes actin turnover, while inactivated cofilin suppresses actin turnover (Figure 2D; Bamburg et al., 2021; Edwards et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about cofilin function, supported by citations.

claim: The maturation of dendritic spines depends on the F/G-actin ratio.
source: The maturation of dendritic spines depends on the F/G-actin ratio (Chen et al., 2007; Rex et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The mushroom spine is a more mature form that typically transmits nerve signals to other neurons compared with the filopodia spine.
source: Compared with the filopodia spine, the mushroom spine is a more mature form that typically transmits nerve signals to other neurons (Hering and Sheng, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study and represents established knowledge about dendritic spine morphology.

claim: PAK3 mRNA levels are significantly reduced in the hippocampus of subjects affected with depression.
source: PAK3 mRNA levels are significantly reduced in the hippocampus of subjects affected with depression (Fuchsova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: In post-mortem brains of Down syndrome and AD patients, PAK3 proteins are markedly reduced with abnormal cofilin activation in neurites.
source: Additionally, in post-mortem brains of Down syndrome and AD patients, PAK3 proteins are markedly reduced with abnormal cofilin activation in neurites (Lauterborn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: PAK3 controls the surface trafficking of the major excitatory receptor GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit in neurons.
source: For example, PAK3 controls the surface trafficking of the major excitatory receptor GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit in neurons (Hussain et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: PAK3 can control synaptic GABA(A)R surface stability via G protein-coupled receptor kinase interacting with ArfGAP 1/βPIX signaling.
source: PAK3 can also control synaptic GABA(A)R surface stability via G protein-coupled receptor kinase interacting with ArfGAP 1/βPIX signaling (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Intranasal administration can bypass the blood-brain barrier and rapidly deliver drugs from the nasal mucosa to the brain in a non-invasive way and reducing systemic side effects.
source: Intranasal administration can bypass the blood-brain barrier and rapidly deliver drugs from the nasal mucosa to the brain in a non-invasive way and reducing systemic side effects (Corrigan et al., 2015; Tucker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge about intranasal drug delivery.

claim: Intranasal insulin administration is used for the treatment of CNS disorders including mild cognitive impairment and AD.
source: Recent studies reported that intranasal insulin administration for the treatment of CNS disorders including mild cognitive impairment and AD (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01767909, Craft et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a clinical trial and published study.

claim: Intranasal administration of microRNA is effective in ischemic brain injury, depression, and AD.
source: Additionally, previous studies reported that intranasal administration of microRNA is effective in ischemic brain injury (Lawson et al., 2022), depression (Guan et al., 2021), and AD (Mai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Drug absorption through the nasal cavity is more efficient than through the gastrointestinal tract.
source: A previous study reported that drug absorption through the nasal cavity is more efficient than through the gastrointestinal tract (Furubayashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Intranasal administration of biomacromolecular agents, including nucleic acid-based drugs, remarkably reduced the degradation rate and increased the delivery efficiency compared to the oral route.
source: In addition, intranasal administration of biomacromolecular agents, including nucleic acid-based drugs, remarkably reduced the degradation rate and increased the delivery efficiency compared to the oral route (Fortuna et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: IR does not induce PAK3 expression by regulating transcription levels.
source: In murine neurons, IR failed to induce any change in luciferase activity (Figure 5A), suggesting that IR does not induce PAK3 expression by regulating transcription levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PAK3 could regulate the F/G-actin ratio and maturation of the dendritic spine through LIMK1-cofilin signaling.
source: These results suggested that PAK3 could regulate the F/G-actin ratio and maturation of the dendritic spine through LIMK1-cofilin signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing PAK3 knockdown and overexpression effects on F/G-actin ratio and dendritic spine morphology.

claim: Upregulation of PAK3 expression could restore the F/G-actin ratio and dendritic spine distribution to normal levels in murine neurons.
source: Considering IR-induced decreased PAK3 signaling, upregulation of PAK3 expression could restore the F/G-actin ratio and dendritic spine distribution to normal levels in murine neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PAK3 overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: PAK3 signaling is essential for the maturation of dendritic spines.
source: Collectively, PAK3 signaling is essential for the maturation of dendritic spines, and IR could disrupt PAK3 signaling in human neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in human differentiated neurons showing PAK3 effects on dendritic spine morphology.

claim: IR could disrupt PAK3 signaling in human neurons.
source: Collectively, PAK3 signaling is essential for the maturation of dendritic spines, and IR could disrupt PAK3 signaling in human neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing IR effects on PAK3 and downstream signaling in human neurons.

claim: IR-induced miR-206-3p decreased PAK3 signaling and dendritic spine maturation in mouse and human neurons.
source: These results suggested that IR-induced miR-206–3 p decreased PAK3 signaling and dendritic spine maturation in mouse and human neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing miR-206-3p effects on PAK3 signaling and dendritic spines.

claim: AntagomiR could be an effective strategy for IR-induced cognitive impairment by restoring PAK3 signaling.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that antagomiR could be an effective strategy for IR-induced cognitive impairment by restoring PAK3 signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experiments showing antagomiR effects on cognitive function and PAK3 signaling.

claim: Cranial irradiation reduced cognitive function and downregulated the expression of PAK3 in the frontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: Our results revealed that cranial irradiation reduced cognitive function and downregulated the expression of PAK3, a gene involved in dendritic spine development and synaptic plasticity in the frontal cortex and hippocampus.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The PAK3-LIMK1-cofilin signaling pathway was affected by IR, leading to dendritic spine maturation impairment.
source: We demonstrated that the PAK3-LIMK1-cofilin signaling pathway was affected by IR, leading to dendritic spine maturation impairment.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by Western blot and imaging data showing effects on the signaling pathway and dendritic spines.

claim: miR-206-3p regulated PAK3 expression.
source: Additionally, we found that miR-206–3 p regulated PAK3 expression and that antagomiR-206–3 p treatment restored PAK3 levels and cognitive function in the irradiated mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing miR-206-3p effects on PAK3 mRNA and protein levels.
